surges.name: The 'Industrial Revolution' (mechanisation and water transport)

big_bang.confidence: HIGH for year and country (Perez 2009 Table 1; Perez & Murray Leach 2022 Table 2); MEDIUM for event wording (Perez 2002 Table 2.1 as reproduced by Stratechery 2021, book not opened)

surges.key_factor: Perez 1985: 'low cost machine-tending and cotton growing labor' ('it could be argued'). Later summaries associate the surge with mechanised cotton, water power and canals; Perez's later texts do not name a single cheap input for surge 1.
paradigm_principles: Factory production; division of labour; efficiency

installation.note: DERIVED: big bang to collapse year. Perez & Murray Leach 2022 Table 1 dates the whole surge 1771-1828.

turning_point.institutional_changes: Not specified in the Perez texts opened for this research; Perez says each turning point brings regulation of finance and a recomposition of the socio-institutional framework.

deployment.note: DERIVED from Perez's surge dating (1771-1828) and the 1793-97 recession.

surges.name: Age of Steam and Railways
surges.core_country: Britain (UK), spreading to the Continent and USA

big_bang.event: Test of the 'Rocket' steam engine for the Liverpool-Manchester railway
big_bang.confidence: HIGH for year (Perez 2009, 2016, 2022); MEDIUM for event wording (book Table 2.1 via Stratechery 2021)

surges.key_factor: Cheap coal (and steam-powered transport). Perez 1985: 'low-cost coal and steam-powered transportation'; Perez 2004: 'abundance of cheap coal'; Perez 2017: 'cheap coal of the second, the iron railway age'.
industries: Steam engines and machinery (made in iron; fuelled by coal)
Steam power for many industries (including textiles)
infrastructures: Great ports, great depots and worldwide sailing ships
paradigm_principles: Economies of agglomeration / industrial cities / national markets
Interdependent movement (of machines and of means of transport)
Free markets as the ideal context

frenzy_bubble.name: Railway mania (UK)
frenzy_bubble.scale: At the 1847 peak UK railway investment reached about 7% of national income and nearly 55% of gross national fixed capital formation (Perez 2009, citing Mitchell 1964 and Deane 1968).

turning_point.institutional_changes: Not detailed in the texts opened; Perez 2025 calls the late-1840s UK turning point a time of 'slow and very uneven growth'.

deployment.note: Victorian boom dated 1850-1873 by Perez (Lebdioui interview, 2025). Perez & Murray Leach 2022 date the surge 1829-1874.

sources: Perez (2009) double bubble, Table 1 and p.8

Lebdioui (2025) A conversation with Carlota Perez, Development and Change, DOI 10.1111/dech.70007 - https://carlotaperez.org/wp-content/downloads/media/interviews-and-podcasts/as-interviewee/Development-and-Change-2025-Lebdioui.pdf

surges.name: Age of Steel, Electricity and Heavy Engineering (civil, chemical, electrical and naval); first globalisation
surges.core_country: USA and Germany (overtaking Britain); Perez 2009 lists U.K., USA and Germany

big_bang.event: Carnegie Bessemer steel plant opens in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
big_bang.confidence: HIGH (Perez 2009 text names 'Carnegie's Bessemer Steel mill'; Perez 2016)

surges.key_factor: Cheap steel. Perez 2004: 'the Bessemer and Siemens Martin processes that made steel as cheap as iron'; Perez 1985 footnote: these processes 'slashed its cost to a tenth'. Perez 2024 explicitly treats electricity as a revolutionary technology inside this surge, dependent on cheap steel.
industries: Full development of the steam engine for steel ships
infrastructures: Worldwide shipping in rapid steel steamships (Suez Canal)
Worldwide railways (cheap steel rails and bolts in standard sizes)
paradigm_principles: Economies of scale of plant / vertical integration
Cost accounting for control and efficiency
Great scale for world market power / 'small' is successful, if local

installation.note: DERIVED: big bang to start of the 1890-93 collapses.

frenzy_bubble.name: Multiple bubbles from the build-up of world infrastructure for global commodity trade (steel railways, steamships, ports, telegraph), financed mainly from the City of London
frenzy_bubble.scale: From the 1870s to the 1890s between 30% and 50% of all British investment went overseas (Perez 2009, citing Davis and Gallman 2001).

turning_point.institutional_changes: Progressive Era reforms in the US (deployment named 'Progressive Era' by Perez); details not in the texts opened.

deployment.note: Belle Epoque; Perez notes 'an overlap of more than a decade between Deployment 3 and Installation 4'. Lebdioui interview prints the Belle Epoque as 1871-1914 (likely a typo for 1891 or similar).

sources: Perez (2004) Technological revolutions, paradigm shifts and socio-institutional change - https://carlotaperez.org/wp-content/downloads/publications/organizational-change/TRs_TEP_shifts_and_SIF_ch.pdf

surges.name: Age of Oil, the Automobile and Mass Production

big_bang.event: First Model-T produced at Ford's plant in Detroit, Michigan
big_bang.confidence: HIGH (Perez 2016: 'In 1908, with the launch of Ford's Model-T')

surges.key_factor: Cheap oil and energy (with petrochemicals / energy-intensive materials). Perez 1985: 'low-cost oil and energy-intensive materials, especially petrochemicals'; Perez 2017: 'oil, electricity and plastic materials'.
industries: Internal combustion engine for automobiles, transport, tractors, aeroplanes, war tanks and electricity
infrastructures: Networks of roads, highways, ports and airports
Worldwide analogue telecommunications (telephone, telex and cablegram), wire and wireless
paradigm_principles: Economies of scale (product and market volume) / horizontal integration
National powers, world agreements and confrontations

frenzy_bubble.name: Roaring Twenties (autos, housing, radio, aviation, electricity)

turning_point.institutional_changes: Keynesian demand management, recognition of unions and collective bargaining, social security, welfare state, Bretton Woods, IMF, World Bank, UN, GATT, Marshall Plan (Perez 2004); 'suburbanization, the Cold War, the welfare state, and the Bretton Woods international stability framework' (Perez 2024).

deployment.note: Perez gives the post-war boom as 1945-71 (Project Syndicate 2024) and 1950-1973 (Lebdioui 2025). Perez & Murray Leach 2022 date the surge 1908-1970.

surges.golden_age: Post-war golden age (US 'American Way of Life'; welfare state)
sources: Perez (2024) What is AI's place in history? Project Syndicate

surges.name: Age of Information and (Tele)communications (ICT); second globalisation
surges.core_country: USA, spreading to Europe and Asia

big_bang.event: Intel microprocessor announced in Santa Clara, California
big_bang.confidence: HIGH (Perez 2016: 'in 1971, the year that Intel's microprocessor was launched')

surges.key_factor: Cheap microelectronics (chips) and, consequently, information. Perez 1985: 'This conjunction of characteristics holds today for microelectronics'; Perez 2017: 'Presently, the low-cost inputs are microelectronics, and, consequently, information'.
industries: Artificial intelligence, robotics, Internet of Things (added in Perez & Murray Leach 2022)
infrastructures: World digital telecommunications (cable, fibre optics, radio and satellite)
Internet / electronic mail and other e-services
High-speed physical transport links (land, air, water)
paradigm_principles: Segmentation of markets / proliferation of niches
Economies of scope and specialisation combined with scale
Globalisation / interaction between the global and the local
Instant contact and action / instant global communications

installation.end: 2000 (first collapse) / 2008 (second); Perez 2022-2025 says installation and turning point have both broken length records
installation.note: Perez 2022: 'we seem to be stuck in the installation period or in what I call the turning point'.

frenzy_bubble.name: Double bubble: Internet / NASDAQ mania (1990s) followed by the easy-liquidity / global financial casino and housing boom (2004-07)
frenzy_bubble.scale: Venture capital funds reached as much as 1% of US GDP at the peak, 85-90% to ICT; technology stocks reached as much as 35% of total market capitalisation, Internet alone almost 10% (Perez 2009). Precursor mini-booms collapsed in 1983 and 1987.

turning_point.years: 2000-03 and 2008-'20??' (Perez 2016 Figure 1); still ongoing per Perez 2022 and 2025
turning_point.institutional_changes: Perez: post-crash rescues (TARP, QE) were not accompanied by recoupling of finance to production, so the turning point has not been completed (Perez 2022 IIPP blog; Lebdioui 2025).

deployment.note: Not yet begun on Perez's reading. She calls the possible golden age 'Sustainable, global, ICT golden Age?' (SPRU slides, 20 Jun 2025) and 'a smart, green, fair and global golden age' (Lebdioui 2025).

surges.golden_age: Not yet: a possible 'sustainable global knowledge society boom' (2009) / 'smart, green, fair and global golden age' (2016-2025)
sources: Perez (14 Jun 2022) A long delayed golden age, IIPP blog - https://carlotaperez.org/wp-content/downloads/media/articles-and-blogs/CP-Why-such-a-long-installation-of-ICT.pdf
Perez (20 Jun 2025) SPRU PhD day lecture slides - https://carlotaperez.org/wp-content/downloads/lectures/Perez-SPRU-PhD-day-2025-lecture-final.pdf

key_factor_criteria_1985: (1) clearly perceived low - and descending - relative cost
(2) apparently unlimited supply (for all practical purposes)
(3) obvious potential for all-pervasive influence in the productive sphere
(4) a generally recognized capacity, based on a set of interwoven technical and organizational innovations, to reduce the costs and change the quality of capital equipment, labor and products
framework_constants.key_factor_criteria_source: Perez (1985) World Development 13(3), pp.441-463, p.6-7 of carlotaperez.org PDF (HIGH; the PDF prints 'for ah practical purposes', an OCR error for 'all')
framework_constants.revolution_criteria_2025: Three features: (1) capacity to increase productivity and reduce costs across the economy; (2) strong synergy among the knowledge bases and skills; (3) provision of a new infrastructure (Lebdioui 2025, HIGH)

durations.whole_surge: 'fifty to sixty years fully to deploy (and exhaust)' (Perez 2009); 'half a century or more' (Perez 2016); 'between forty and sixty years' (Perez 2022)
durations.installation: 'two or three decades' (Perez 2009); 'may last 20-30 years or more' (Perez 2017)
durations.turning_point: 'a recessive period that can last anywhere from two to thirteen years or more' (Perez 2017)

perez_on_ai.quote: Rather than seeing an information age beginning in the 1970s with the widespread application of the microprocessor, the spread of computers, and the advent of the internet, as I would, they take the start of their new machine age from an advanced stage of these technologies: i.e. with robotics and artificial intelligence.
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, 'Second Machine Age or Fifth Technological Revolution? (Part 3)', carlotaperez.org (Beyond the Technological Revolution series)

perez_on_ai.quote: the next revolutionary technological shift may be driven by biotech, nanotech or some still unidentified combination
Artificial intelligence, Robotics, Internet of Things [listed under FIFTH: From 1971, Age of Information and Telecommunications, 'New technologies and new or redefined industries']
perez_on_ai.source: Perez & Murray Leach, BEYOND4.0 D7.1, Table 2 (adapted from Perez 2002 Tables 2.2-2.3)

perez_on_ai.quote: after four revolutions replacing manual labour, the new technologies have found an enormous new territory to mechanise: mental labour!
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, 'A long delayed golden age: Or why has the ICT installation period lasted so long?', IIPP blog (Medium)

perez_on_ai.quote: Everyone is talking about artificial intelligence as though it represents the next technological revolution. In fact, it is better understood as a key development within the still-evolving information-communications-technology (ICT) revolution, which started in the 1970s with the microprocessor.
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, 'What Is AI's Place in History?', Project Syndicate (also PS Spring Quarterly 2024, pp.26-31)

perez_on_ai.quote: AI may plausibly evolve as a third leap. But what is most important to recognize today is that ICT has already brought us to the threshold of a golden age.
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, What Is AI's Place in History? (author's PDF)

perez_on_ai.quote: But a revolutionary technology is not the same thing as a technological revolution.
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, What Is AI's Place in History?

perez_on_ai.quote: the latest advances in AI are analogous to the introduction of plastics mid-way through the mass-production revolution.
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, What Is AI's Place in History?

perez_on_ai.quote: AI is certain to become an integral part of the current digital revolution, and it could also lay the groundwork for breakthroughs in biotech, nanotech, and other fields that may be at the center of an eventual sixth revolution.
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, What Is AI's Place in History?

perez_on_ai.quote: But if AI's development unfolds in a system where financial markets remain unregulated and decoupled from the real economy, it is unlikely to move us in a more environmentally, socially, or politically sustainable direction.
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, What Is AI's Place in History?

perez_on_ai.quote: AND FOR THE CURRENT ICT REVOLUTION: Microprocessors and computers/ Internet/ Artificial intelligence and much more still to come
perez_on_ai.source: Perez, 'The world is at a crossroads: It is time for understanding institutional innovation', SPRU PhD day lecture slides (slide 10)

perez_on_ai.quote: I have not seen a golden age happening without a crash
perez_on_ai.source: John Thornhill, 'Brace for a crash before the golden age of AI', Financial Times (syndicated by The Irish Times as 'Before the golden age of AI must come the crash, history suggests', 23 Aug 2025)
perez_on_ai.confidence: HIGH (read in the Irish Times syndication; FT original not opened)

perez_on_ai.quote: This could also be a trigger for gigantic instability
perez_on_ai.source: Thornhill, FT via The Irish Times (Perez on the bursting of the AI bubble amid misfiring capital markets and global debt above three times GDP)

perez_on_ai.quote: Having understood both the beneficial potential and the perils of the information technology revolution, including artificial intelligence (AI) as the latest addition, it is possible for the state to provide directionality towards constructing a smart, green, fair and global golden age
perez_on_ai.source: Amir Lebdioui, 'A Conversation with Carlota Perez: A Life of Revolutions', Development and Change (2025), DOI 10.1111/dech.70007

perez_on_ai.quote: But we are late. This time the record in length has been broken, for both the installation and the turning point itself. The good news is that we could have a golden age ahead; the bad news is that we are not doing very much towards achieving it.
there is also a financial crisis in the making with world debt at almost four times global GDP
The first thing to understand is that green technologies are not a revolution; they are a set of different solutions to a very serious problem that must be confronted.

counter_views.position: A 'second machine age' replacing brain power began recently; Perez counters that this mistakes the ICT turning point for an inflection point.

Journalist's framing: 'As for AI, we remain in that manic installation phase'; also notes AI is 'the first revolution to be driven by software as much as hardware'. Reports Perez 'sees AI as an extension of that fifth technological revolution'.

counter_views.who: Ben Thompson, Stratechery - 'The Benefits of Bubbles'
counter_views.position: Uses Perez to argue bubbles install capacity; worries that GPU spending is short-lived relative to railways or fibre ('Chips break down and get superseded'); sees power generation as the Perez-style lasting infrastructure. A March 2026 follow-up ('Agents Over Bubbles') reportedly says he no longer believes AI is a bubble (not opened).
counter_views.quote: The problem from a Perez perspective is that all of this spending on chips is, relative to the sort of infrastructure she wrote about — railroads, factories, fiber, etc. — short-lived.

counter_views.who: Jerry Neumann - 'AI Will Not Make You Rich' (The Colossus Review)
counter_views.position: Asks whether generative AI is like ICT (value captured by startups) or shipping containerisation (value spread thin to consumers); search summaries say he concludes value will largely flow to users/consumers, consistent with a late-cycle (deployment-type) technology. Essay text not opened; only his reactionwheel.net pointer post was read.
counter_views.quote: Is generative AI more like the former or the latter? Will it be the basis of many future industrial fortunes, or a net loser for the investment community as a whole, with a few zero-sum winners here and there?
counter_views.confidence: HIGH for the setup quote; MEDIUM for the conclusion

counter_views.who: Azeem Azhar, Exponential View - 'AI: Boom or Bubble' five-gauge framework
counter_views.position: Five gauges (economic strain/investment intensity, industry strain capex vs revenue, revenue momentum, valuation heat, funding quality) grounded in Perez and Bill Janeway; classified the AI build-out as a boom rather than a bubble (per search summaries). Primary page returned 404 during research.

counter_views.who: Benedict Evans - 'AI eats the world' presentations
counter_views.position: AI is the biggest platform shift since the iPhone 'but only that'; 'World changing things tend to lead bubbles. So yeah, if we're not in a bubble now, we will be' (quote from search summaries of the a16z podcast; not opened).
counter_views.verified: partial (presentations page opened; quote not verified)

counter_views.position: Nvidia run-rate data-centre revenue x2 (for total data-centre cost) implies AI needs about $600B a year of revenue to justify the build-out; revenue falls far short. Page redirected to a host not allowed in this session.

counter_views.who: Goldman Sachs Global Macro Research - Top of Mind issue 129, 'Gen AI: too much spend, too little benefit?'
counter_views.position: Tech giants and others to spend 'an estimated ~$1tn on capex in coming years' with 'little to show for it so far' (HIGH, page opened). Inside: Jim Covello sceptical; Joseph Briggs estimates AI could raise US productivity 9% and GDP 6.1% over ten years (MEDIUM, from search summaries).

counter_views.who: Daron Acemoglu - 'The Simple Macroeconomics of AI'
counter_views.position: Task-based estimate: 'no more than a 0.71% increase in total factor productivity over 10 years', and 'predicted to be less than 0.55%' once hard-to-learn tasks are considered.

counter_views.who: IMF - World Economic Outlook / Global Financial Stability Report
counter_views.position: Chief economist Gourinchas: 'echoes in the current tech investment surge of the dot-com boom of the late 1990s'; AI-related investment up by under 0.4% of US GDP since 2022 vs 1.2% in 1995-2000; a bust less likely to be systemic because largely equity- and cash-funded. imf.org returned 403.

M7 share of S&P 500 market cap grew to nearly 35% from about 20% in November 2022; M7 P/E approaching top 10% of history but 'still well below the levels reached at the peak of the dotcom bubble'; other tech firms' valuations 'approaching the levels reached at the peak of the dotcom bubble'. Rally underpinned by earnings, 'dissimilar to the dotcom bubble'.

'a wave of optimism about AI spurred a surge in capital expenditure on AI infrastructure' and 'animal spirits about AI lifted stock valuations'. Press coverage (not opened) says BIS compared the boom to 1840s railway mania, 1920s electrification and the dot-com era without calling it a bubble.
counter_views.confidence: HIGH for quoted lines; MEDIUM for press characterisation

counter_views.who: Commentators collected on Perez's own press page (2026)
counter_views.position: Michael Wee (Aug 2026): 'this AI wave is now deep in the installation phase'; Gunther Schnabl (Jul 2026) on financial vs productive capital driving the AI bubble; James Görgen (Sep 2026) 'Why should we want the AI bubble to burst?'. These read AI as a sixth-surge installation/frenzy (interpretation A), contrary to Perez's own placement.

A.label: AI = sixth surge, now in installation (irruption/frenzy)
A.strongest_argument: AI fits Perez's 2002 definition of a revolution more than any single ICT product: a cluster (models, accelerators, data centres, power) with a key input whose cost at fixed capability falls 9x-900x a year (Epoch, Mar 2025), a new infrastructure (GW-scale data centres, ~$448B big-five capex in 2025), and visibly 'frenzy' finance: AI took ~72% of global VC (Jan-Sep 2026), 82.7% of US VC deal value, valuations near $1T for private labs, supplier/circular financing, SPVs and private credit. Mechanising mental labour is a different 'territory' from four revolutions of manual labour (Perez 2022).
A.weaknesses: Perez says the opposite; the key input is still microelectronics; the infrastructure rides on the internet and cloud; incumbents (the fifth surge's giants) lead rather than new entrants; and if 2022 is the big bang, a major frenzy four years in would be historically early (big bang to crash averaged ~21 years) - more like a 'precursor bubble' (ICT had them in 1983 and 1987).

B.label: AI = late chapter ('third leap') of the fifth (ICT) surge
B.strongest_argument: This is Perez's own published position (Project Syndicate, 11 Mar 2024; FT 23 Aug 2025 as reported; Development and Change, Oct 2025; SPRU slides, Jun 2025). AI 'depends on the internet, which in turn depends on powerful microprocessors and computers'; she lists AI among the fifth surge's industries (2022). The key factor is still ever-cheaper chips (Epoch: AI chip performance per dollar +49%/yr since 2023); the paradigm principles AI intensifies (information intensity, data as raw material, platforms) are those of ICT; the leaders are ICT incumbents funding capex largely from cash flow. Her plastics and electricity analogies are revolutionary technologies within a surge, and she reads the present as an over-long turning point awaiting institutional recomposition.
B.weaknesses: Under B the AI boom is a third bubble inside a turning point that began in 2000/2008 - a pattern with no precedent in the first four surges; B struggles to explain why finance is re-coupling with a production build-out on this scale (capex ~1.5% of US GDP) without any new regulatory settlement.

C.label: Hybrid: AI as a revolutionary technology inside ICT whose financial dynamics replay installation, and possible forerunner of a sixth surge
C.strongest_argument: Perez herself leaves the door open: AI 'could also lay the groundwork for breakthroughs in biotech, nanotech, and other fields that may be at the center of an eventual sixth revolution' (2024). Her own precedent of Bessemer steel in the 1860s - a revolutionary technology midway through surge 2 that became the key factor of surge 3 - fits AI exactly: a technology emerging inside a mature paradigm, attracting a mini-frenzy, and possibly becoming the cheap input of the next. Data support both halves: the cost-of-capability collapse and frenzy indicators (A) coexist with incumbent leadership, chip dependence and modest measured productivity (B).
C.weaknesses: Hard to falsify; risks having it both ways. Needs an explicit test: whether a non-ICT cluster (AI x biotech x materials) with its own infrastructure and cheap input emerges.
C.status: DERIVED analysis, textually supported by Perez 2024

ai_mapping.perez_own_position: B (with a C-type caveat). Verbatim: 'it is better understood as a key development within the still-evolving information-communications-technology (ICT) revolution' and 'AI may plausibly evolve as a third leap' (Project Syndicate, 11 Mar 2024); 'the information technology revolution, including artificial intelligence (AI) as the latest addition' (Development and Change, Oct 2025). On the boom: 'I have not seen a golden age happening without a crash' (FT, 23 Aug 2025).
